lists.notes: Looping over lists (deferred by B04) is lists.loop_over_items / loop_over_indexes; they encompass the B04 loop_patterns. split/join (B03 request) are encompassed by lists.text_to_list_and_back, which depends on list_methods.append_build. list(range()), len(range) and list('str') are in membership_and_operators KP4. sum()/min()/max() on lists are B05 builtin_functions, which should encompass lists.loop_over_items. Lists of lists / 2D grids are B07 nested_data_structures (copying.shallow_vs_deep only previews double indexing). Lists as function parameters live in mutability_aliasing.lists_in_functions. random.choice on lists is B13 random_module. Sequence patterns in match (case [x, y]) were not added; B07 or a stitching pass may add them. Reconciliation: len/sum/max/min of a list (the B05/B06 gap) is lists.aggregate_builtins; later topics that apply these built-ins to lists depend on it instead of builtin_functions.sum_max_min.

list_methods.notes: sort()/reverse() are taught in sorting.sort_and_sorted. clear() is mentioned only in mutability_aliasing.lists_in_functions. Using lists as stacks/queues (pop() vs pop(0), deque) is B07 stacks_queues; building lists with comprehensions is B07 list_comprehensions, which should encompass append_build (filter KP).

list_slicing.notes: Builds on B03 string slicing as B03 asked: only what differs for lists (result is a list, slice vs index, slice assignment). Copying with [:] is copying.copy_a_list. slice_assignment is non-core (py4e/Helsinki only). sys.argv[1:] is B10 command_line_args.

tuples.notes: Tuples as dict keys and dict.items() pairs are B07 dictionaries. Returning tuples from functions is unpacking.return_multiple_values. namedtuple is B07 collections_module.

unpacking.notes: B02 variables.swap_values and B03 split_into_parts already preview unpacking; unpack_sequences encompasses them. star_unpacking is non-core and covers *rest and print(*lst) only; *args/**kwargs and ** dict unpacking are B08 args_kwargs. return_multiple_values has pending concept:return_values (B05 runs in parallel); if B05 also wrote a 'return several values' topic, the stitching pass should keep one. Reconciliation: return_multiple_values (duplicate of B05 return_values.multiple_return_values) was replaced by use_returned_tuples, which depends on it.

enumerate_zip.notes: Only 2 courses introduce these, but they are core idioms that replace range(len(...)). dict(zip(keys, values)) is B07 dictionaries; zip(strict=True) and itertools are B07 itertools_module.

mutability_aliasing.notes: lists_in_functions needs def/parameters, so it has pending concept:parameters_arguments (B05 runs in parallel); it includes the mutable default argument gotcha. Aliasing of objects/attributes is the OOP batch (B11). Integer/string interning is deliberately not taught; is is presented as 'only for None'.

copying.notes: shallow_vs_deep is non-core and previews lists of lists, which B07 nested_data_structures owns; it uses `import copy` before B13 modules_imports, as a single memorised line. Copying dicts (dict.copy) is B07.

sorting.notes: key= is taught only with existing functions (len, str.lower). key=lambda and key=<own function> belong to B08 lambda_functions / higher_order_functions, which should encompass sort_tuples_and_keys. Sorting dict items by value is B07 dictionaries (py4e 'sorting a dictionary using tuples'). Sorting algorithms (bubble, merge sort) are a later algorithms batch.

topics.title: Making a list and reading items by index
topics.summary: Write a list literal, read items with positive and negative indexes, get its length, and recognise IndexError.

knowledge_points.title: A list holds several values in order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 92]
names = ['Ana', 'Bo']
empty = []
print(scores)  # [70, 85, 92]
Square brackets, items separated by commas; a list can hold any type, or nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what print shows for short lists, including an empty list and a list mixing strings and numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 92]
print(scores[0])   # 70
print(scores[-1])  # 92
Exactly the same rules as indexing characters in a string.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the item at given positive and negative indexes; write the index expression for 'second item' and 'last item'.

knowledge_points.title: len() counts the items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 92]
print(len(scores))              # 3
print(scores[len(scores) - 1])  # 92
The last valid index is len - 1, because counting starts at 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() of lists of different sizes (including []); give the last valid index.

knowledge_points.title: Indexing past the end raises IndexError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 92]
print(scores[3])
# IndexError: list index out of range
Valid indexes for 3 items are 0, 1, 2 and -1, -2, -3.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which index expressions raise IndexError; fix an off-by-one index that uses len(scores).

topics.title: Changing items in a list
topics.summary: Replace an item by assigning to its index, update it from its own value, and see why this works for lists but not strings.

knowledge_points.title: Assign to an index to replace an item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue']
colors[1] = 'yellow'
print(colors)  # ['red', 'yellow', 'blue']
The list itself changes; its length stays the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after one or two index assignments, including a negative index.

knowledge_points.title: Update an item from its own value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 92]
scores[0] += 5
scores[-1] = scores[-1] - 2
print(scores)  # [75, 85, 90]
Read the old item, compute, write it back, just like x += 5 for a variable.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a short sequence of updates; fill in the line that doubles the second item.

knowledge_points.title: Lists are mutable, strings are not
knowledge_points.worked_example:
word = 'cat'
# word[0] = 'b'  -> TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
letters = ['c', 'a', 't']
letters[0] = 'b'
print(letters)  # ['b', 'a', 't']
A list can be changed in place; a string must be rebuilt.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which snippets run and which raise TypeError; predict the result of the ones that run.

knowledge_points.title: You cannot assign past the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85]
# scores[2] = 99  -> IndexError: list assignment index out of range
print(len(scores))  # 2
Assignment only replaces existing items; adding a new item needs append (next topics).
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the line that raises IndexError in a short program.

topics.title: Checking membership and combining lists
topics.summary: Use in / not in, +, * and == with lists, and turn a range or a string into a list with list().

knowledge_points.title: in and not in test whether an item is present
knowledge_points.worked_example:
fruits = ['apple', 'pear']
print('pear' in fruits)      # True
print('kiwi' not in fruits)  # True
if 'apple' in fruits:
    print('Have apples')
For a list, in matches whole items, not parts of strings: 'pe' in fruits is False.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict True/False for membership tests, including a partial string; write an if that warns when an item is missing.

knowledge_points.title: + joins lists, * repeats them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
b = [3]
print(a + b)      # [1, 2, 3]
print([0] * 4)    # [0, 0, 0, 0]
print(a)          # [1, 2]  (unchanged)
Both build a new list, exactly like + and * on strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the results of + and * on small lists; spot the error in [1, 2] + 3 (TypeError: can only concatenate list).

knowledge_points.title: == compares lists item by item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print([1, 2, 3] == [1, 2, 3])  # True
print([1, 2, 3] == [3, 2, 1])  # False
print([1, 2] != [1, 2, 0])     # True
Same items in the same order means equal; order matters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of == and != on pairs of lists that differ in order, length or one item.

knowledge_points.title: list() turns a range or a string into a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(list(range(1, 5)))  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list('hey'))        # ['h', 'e', 'y']
print(len(range(0, 10, 2)))  # 5
list() collects every value a for loop would visit.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict list(range(...)) for start/stop/step combinations and list() of short strings.

topics.title: Looping over the items of a list
topics.summary: Visit every item with for item in list and apply the total, count and largest-so-far patterns to a list.

knowledge_points.title: for visits each item in order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pets = ['cat', 'dog', 'fish']
for pet in pets:
    print('I have a', pet)
The loop variable holds each item in turn, as with characters of a string.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of loops over short lists; write a loop that prints each item in upper case.

knowledge_points.title: Total and average of a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
prices = [4, 10, 6]
total = 0
for p in prices:
    total += p
print(total, total / len(prices))  # 20 6.666666666666667
The accumulator pattern, now fed by a list instead of input().
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that totals a list; compute an average and guard against an empty list.

knowledge_points.title: Count items that pass a test
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = [18, 25, 31, 22, 29]
hot = 0
for t in temps:
    if t > 24:
        hot += 1
print(hot)  # 3
Counting is the accumulator with an if inside.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the counter for a given list; write a loop that counts words starting with a given letter.

knowledge_points.title: Largest so far, starting from the first item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = [18, 25, 31, 22]
best = temps[0]
for t in temps:
    if t > best:
        best = t
print(best)  # 31
Starting from temps[0] avoids the 'start at 0' bug for all-negative lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the smallest-so-far version; pick the correct starting value for a list of negative numbers.

topics.title: len, sum, max and min on a list
topics.summary: Summarise a list with len(), sum(), max() and min(), compute an average, guard against empty lists, and know what these built-ins do with lists of strings.

knowledge_points.title: One call instead of a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 85, 90]
print(len(scores), sum(scores), max(scores), min(scores))  # 3 245 90 70
The same built-ins you used with ranges and several arguments accept a whole list; each replaces an accumulator or largest-so-far loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len/sum/max/min of given lists; rewrite accumulator and max-tracking loops as one call.

knowledge_points.title: Average: sum divided by len
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 80, 90]
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))  # 80.0
The average is always a float; round it only when you display it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the average of a list; fix code that divides by a hard-coded count instead of len().

knowledge_points.title: Empty lists: sum is 0, max and min fail
knowledge_points.worked_example:
empty = []
print(sum(empty), len(empty))  # 0 0
if len(empty) > 0:
    print(max(empty))
else:
    print("no scores")  # no scores
print(max(empty))  # ValueError: max() iterable argument is empty
There is no largest item of nothing (and an average would divide by zero), so check the length first.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results and errors for empty lists; add a guard to an average or max function that crashes on [].

knowledge_points.title: Lists of strings: max and min go by alphabet, sum fails
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["pear", "apple", "fig"]
print(max(words), min(words))  # pear apple
sum(words)  # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
max and min use the same ordering as < on strings; sum only adds numbers.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict max/min of word lists (including capitals); classify calls as working or raising TypeError.

topics.notes: Added in reconciliation: B05 builtin_functions.sum_max_min used only ranges and several arguments (lists were in parallel B06), and B06 wrote the loops by hand. Snippets run with Python 3.13.

topics.title: Looping over positions with range(len(...))
topics.summary: Loop over indexes when you need the position: change items in place, compare neighbours, and walk two lists in step.

knowledge_points.title: for i in range(len(items)) gives each index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy']
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(i, names[i])
# 0 Ana / 1 Bo / 2 Cy
Use this form when the position itself matters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed index/item pairs; fill in range(...) so the loop covers every index.

knowledge_points.title: Changing every item needs the index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
for n in nums:
    n = n * 10      # only changes the loop variable
print(nums)         # [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(nums)):
    nums[i] = nums[i] * 10
print(nums)         # [10, 20, 30]
Assigning to the loop variable never touches the list; assign to nums[i].
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after each kind of loop; fix a loop that tries to modify items through the loop variable.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing neighbours: stop one early
knowledge_points.practice: Find the IndexError in a neighbour loop that uses range(len(temps)); write a loop that checks a list is sorted.

knowledge_points.title: Two lists in step with one index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['Ana', 'Bo']
scores = [91, 78]
for i in range(len(names)):
    print(names[i], scores[i])
Parallel lists share positions; enumerate and zip (later) make this tidier.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop printing matching items from two lists; predict output when one list is shorter (IndexError).

topics.title: From text to a list and back: split, process, join
topics.summary: Split a line of text into a list, convert or filter its items into a new list, and join the result back into text.

knowledge_points.title: split() gives a list you can loop over
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = 'red green blue'
for word in line.split():
    print(word.upper())
Everything you know about lists applies to the result of split().
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of loops over split() results, including a separator other than space.

knowledge_points.title: Turn text numbers into a list of numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = '4 10 6'
nums = []
for part in line.split():
    nums.append(int(part))
print(nums)  # [4, 10, 6]
split() always gives strings; convert each one before doing arithmetic.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that totals the numbers in a space- or comma-separated line; fix a program that 'adds' '4' + '10'.

knowledge_points.title: Process the words, then join them back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = 'the cat sat'.split()
out = []
for w in words:
    out.append(w.capitalize())
print(' '.join(out))  # The Cat Sat
split -> new list -> join is the standard way to edit text word by word.
knowledge_points.practice: Write split-process-join code for a given transformation (reverse each word, keep long words only).

knowledge_points.title: Joining numbers needs strings first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, 10, 6]
parts = []
for n in nums:
    parts.append(str(n))
print(', '.join(parts))  # 4, 10, 6
', '.join(nums) raises TypeError because join only accepts strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a join that fails on numbers; predict the joined output for different separators.

topics.title: Growing a list with append()
topics.summary: Add items to the end with append, and build a new list in a loop: from a range, by filtering another list, or from user input.

knowledge_points.title: append() adds one item to the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cart = ['milk']
cart.append('eggs')
cart.append('tea')
print(cart)  # ['milk', 'eggs', 'tea']
append changes the list in place; you call it with a dot, like a string method.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after several appends; predict len() afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: Start empty, append in a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
squares = []
for n in range(1, 5):
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)  # [1, 4, 9, 16]
The list version of the accumulator: an empty list instead of 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of a list-building loop; write a loop that builds the first n even numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Filter: append only the items that pass
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = [18, 25, 31, 22]
hot = []
for t in temps:
    if t > 24:
        hot.append(t)
print(hot)  # [25, 31]
The original list is untouched; the answer is a new list.
knowledge_points.practice: Write filters (even numbers, words longer than 3); fix a filter whose empty list is created inside the loop.

knowledge_points.title: Collect input until a stop value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = []
name = input('Name (blank to stop): ')
while name != '':
    names.append(name)
    name = input('Name (blank to stop): ')
print(len(names), 'names')
The sentinel loop now keeps everything it reads, so you can use it afterwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the list for a given sequence of inputs; make sure the stop value itself is not stored.

topics.title: insert(), extend(), and methods that return None
topics.summary: Insert an item at a position, add many items with extend or +=, and avoid the bug of assigning the result of a list method.

knowledge_points.title: insert(i, x) puts x before position i
knowledge_points.worked_example:
queue = ['Bo', 'Cy']
queue.insert(0, 'Ana')
queue.insert(2, 'Di')
print(queue)  # ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Di', 'Cy']
Items from i onwards shift right by one.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after inserts at the start, middle and with an index past the end (it appends).

knowledge_points.title: extend() adds every item; append() adds one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
a.append([3, 4])
print(a)  # [1, 2, [3, 4]]
b = [1, 2]
b.extend([3, 4])
print(b)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
append puts the whole list inside as a single item.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list and its len() after append vs extend; choose the call that gives a target list.

knowledge_points.title: += extends in place; + makes a new list
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both lists after mixed +, += and extend steps.

knowledge_points.title: List methods return None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [1, 2]
items = items.append(3)
print(items)  # None
The list was changed, then the name was pointed at append's return value, None.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the bug in code that assigns the result of append, extend or insert.

topics.title: Removing items: remove(), pop() and del
topics.summary: Remove an item by value or by position, use the value pop returns, and avoid ValueError and IndexError.

knowledge_points.title: remove(x) deletes the first matching value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pets = ['cat', 'dog', 'cat']
pets.remove('cat')
print(pets)  # ['dog', 'cat']
Only the first match goes; the others stay.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after remove calls on lists with duplicates.

knowledge_points.title: remove raises ValueError if the value is absent
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pets = ['dog']
if 'cat' in pets:
    pets.remove('cat')
print(pets)  # ['dog']
# pets.remove('cat') without the check -> ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list
Check with in first when the item might be missing.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot which remove calls crash; guard a remove with an in test.

knowledge_points.title: pop() removes and returns an item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
stack = ['a', 'b', 'c']
last = stack.pop()
first = stack.pop(0)
print(last, first, stack)  # c a ['b']
pop() takes the last item; pop(i) takes position i. Both hand the item back.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the returned values and the remaining list; pop from an empty list (IndexError).

knowledge_points.title: del removes by position; choosing the right tool
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
del nums[1]
print(nums)  # [10, 30]
Know the value: remove. Know the position and need the item: pop. Know the position only: del.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose remove, pop or del for described situations; write the line that deletes the last item.

topics.title: Finding items: index() and count()
topics.summary: Find where a value first appears with index, count how often it appears, and find all positions of a value.

knowledge_points.title: count(x) says how many times x appears
knowledge_points.worked_example:
votes = ['yes', 'no', 'yes', 'yes']
print(votes.count('yes'))  # 3
print(votes.count('maybe'))  # 0
count never fails; a missing value just counts 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts; replace a counting loop with one count call.

knowledge_points.title: index(x) gives the first position
knowledge_points.worked_example:
votes = ['yes', 'no', 'yes']
print(votes.index('no'))   # 1
print(votes.index('yes'))  # 0
Like find() on strings, but for list items.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict index results on lists with repeats.

knowledge_points.title: index raises ValueError: check with in first
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that crashes on a missing value; choose between index and in for a described task.

knowledge_points.title: All positions of a value need a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
votes = ['yes', 'no', 'yes']
spots = []
for i in range(len(votes)):
    if votes[i] == 'yes':
        spots.append(i)
print(spots)  # [0, 2]
index only reports the first match.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the loop that collects every position of a value.

topics.title: Don't remove from a list while looping over it
topics.summary: Recognise the skipped-item bug of removing during a for loop and fix it by building a new list or using while.

knowledge_points.title: The bug: items get skipped
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the (wrong) result of remove-in-loop code for given lists.

knowledge_points.title: Fix 1: build a new list of the items to keep
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
keep = []
for n in nums:
    if n != 2:
        keep.append(n)
nums = keep
print(nums)  # [1, 3]
Reading one list and writing another never skips anything.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a buggy remove loop as a filter loop.

knowledge_points.title: Fix 2: remove until the value is gone
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
while 2 in nums:
    nums.remove(2)
print(nums)  # [1, 3]
Each pass removes one copy; the in test stops the loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which snippets correctly remove all copies of a value.

topics.title: Slicing lists
topics.summary: Apply string slicing to lists, tell a slice (a list) from an index (an item), and use the common first-n / rest / reversed slices.

knowledge_points.title: Same slice rules, now giving a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:3])   # [20, 30]
print(nums[:2])    # [10, 20]
print(nums[-2:])   # [40, 50]
start is included, stop is excluded, exactly as for strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict slices with omitted and negative bounds.

knowledge_points.title: A slice is a list; an index is an item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[1])     # 20
print(nums[1:2])   # [20]
nums[1:2] + 5 fails with TypeError; nums[1] + 5 works.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether each expression gives an item or a list; fix code that adds a number to a one-item slice.

knowledge_points.title: Slices never raise IndexError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[1:100])  # [20, 30]
print(nums[5:])     # []
Out-of-range bounds are clipped; an index that far would crash.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of slices that go past either end, including empty results.

knowledge_points.title: Everyday slices: rest, last n, every other, reversed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:])    # [20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[::2])   # [10, 30, 50]
print(nums[::-1])  # [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
The original list is unchanged; each slice is a new list.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the slice for a described part of a list (all but the first, last three, odd positions, reversed).

topics.title: Changing part of a list with a slice
topics.summary: Replace, insert and delete a range of items with slice assignment and del on a slice.

knowledge_points.title: Assign to a slice to replace a range
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums[1:3] = [20, 30]
print(nums)  # [1, 20, 30, 4, 5]
Unlike reading a slice, assigning to one changes the list itself.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after slice assignments of the same length.

knowledge_points.title: The new part can be longer or shorter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums[1:4] = [0]
print(nums)  # [1, 0, 5]
nums[1:1] = [7, 8]
print(nums)  # [1, 7, 8, 0, 5]
An empty slice like [1:1] inserts without replacing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lengths and contents after shrinking, growing and inserting slice assignments.

knowledge_points.title: del on a slice removes a range
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
del nums[:2]
print(nums)  # [3, 4, 5]
del nums[:]
print(nums)  # []
del nums[:] empties the list but keeps the same list object.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the del statement that removes a described range; compare with remove and pop.

topics.title: Tuples: lists that cannot change
topics.summary: Write tuples (including the one-item tuple), read them like lists, and recognise the TypeError when trying to change one.

knowledge_points.title: A tuple is written with parentheses and read like a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
point = (3, 7)
print(point[0], point[-1])  # 3 7
print(len(point))           # 2
print(7 in point)           # True
Indexing, len, in and slicing all work as for lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict indexing, len and in results on tuples.

knowledge_points.title: Tuples are immutable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
point = (3, 7)
# point[0] = 5  -> TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
point = (5, 7)  # make a new tuple instead
print(point)
Tuples have no append or remove either.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which operations work on a tuple; fix code that tries to change one.

knowledge_points.title: The comma makes the tuple
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = (5)
b = (5,)
c = 1, 2
print(type(a), type(b), type(c))
# <class 'int'> <class 'tuple'> <class 'tuple'>
A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma; parentheses alone are just grouping.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the type of several literals, including (5), (5,), () and 1, 2.

topics.title: Converting and comparing tuples
topics.summary: Convert between lists and tuples, and predict how tuples compare: item by item from the left.

knowledge_points.title: tuple() and list() convert back and forth
knowledge_points.worked_example:
t = (1, 2, 3)
lst = list(t)
lst.append(4)
t = tuple(lst)
print(t)  # (1, 2, 3, 4)
To 'change' a tuple, convert to a list, change it, and convert back.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the results of conversions; write code that adds an item to a tuple's contents.

knowledge_points.title: Tuples compare item by item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print((1, 5) < (2, 0))    # True: 1 < 2 decides
print((1, 5) < (1, 9))    # True: tie, so 5 < 9 decides
print((2, 0) == (2, 0))   # True
The first position that differs decides, just like letters in a word.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict < and == between pairs of tuples, including ties in the first item.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing (hours, minutes) and other records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
start = (9, 45)
end = (10, 5)
print(start < end)  # True
print(('Lee', 3) < ('Li', 1))  # True: 'Lee' < 'Li'
Ordering the fields from most to least important makes comparison do the right thing.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose a field order so that < means 'earlier'; predict comparisons of (name, number) tuples.

topics.title: Lists of tuples as simple records
topics.summary: Store records as tuples in a list, read fields by index in a loop, and choose between a list and a tuple for a job.

knowledge_points.title: A list of (name, score) records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
results = [('Ana', 91), ('Bo', 78)]
print(results[1])     # ('Bo', 78)
print(results[1][0])  # Bo
The first index picks the record, the second picks the field.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of single and double indexing into a list of tuples.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over records and read fields
knowledge_points.practice: Write loops that filter or total records by one field; find the name with the best score.

knowledge_points.title: Append new records as tuples
knowledge_points.worked_example:
results = []
results.append(('Di', 66))
results.append(('Ed', 72))
print(len(results), results[0])  # 2 ('Di', 66)
results.append('Di', 66) is a TypeError: append takes one item, so wrap the fields in a tuple.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix append calls missing the inner parentheses; build a list of (word, length) tuples from a list of words.

knowledge_points.title: List or tuple?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
shopping = ['milk', 'eggs']   # grows and shrinks: list
rgb = (255, 128, 0)          # fixed fields: tuple
Use a list for a collection of similar things; a tuple for one thing with a fixed set of parts.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose list or tuple for described data.

topics.title: Unpacking a tuple or list into names
topics.summary: Assign the items of a tuple or list to several names at once, and understand the swap idiom and the count-mismatch ValueError.

knowledge_points.title: Unpack a tuple into names
knowledge_points.worked_example:
point = (3, 7)
x, y = point
print(x, y)  # 3 7
Names on the left are filled from the items on the right, in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the names' values after unpacking tuples and lists.

knowledge_points.title: The counts must match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x, y = (1, 2, 3)
# ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
Fewer items gives ValueError: not enough values to unpack.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which unpackings raise ValueError; fix the left side to match the data.

knowledge_points.title: Swapping and splitting are unpacking
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a          # the right side is the tuple (2, 1)
day, month = '12/10'.split('/')
print(a, b, day, month)  # 2 1 12 10
1, 2 builds a tuple; the left side unpacks it.
knowledge_points.practice: Explain in one choice why the swap works; write one-line unpacking of a split date.

topics.title: Unpacking records in a for loop
topics.summary: Write for name, score in records to name the fields of each tuple, instead of indexing r[0] and r[1].

knowledge_points.title: Two loop variables for two fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
results = [('Ana', 91), ('Bo', 78)]
for name, score in results:
    print(name, 'scored', score)
Each tuple is unpacked into the two names on every pass.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output; rewrite an r[0]/r[1] loop with unpacking.

knowledge_points.title: Use the named fields in a pattern
knowledge_points.worked_example:
results = [('Ana', 91), ('Bo', 78), ('Cy', 85)]
total = 0
for name, score in results:
    total += score
print(total / len(results))  # 84.66666666666667
Unused fields still need a name; _ is the convention for 'ignored'.
knowledge_points.practice: Write loops that total, filter or find the best record using unpacked names.

knowledge_points.title: Mismatch inside a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
points = [(1, 2), (3, 4, 5)]
for x, y in points:
    print(x + y)
# 3, then ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
Every record must have the same number of fields as loop variables.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the record that breaks a loop; fix the loop variables to match.

topics.title: Collecting the rest with *
topics.summary: Use a starred name to collect leftover items when unpacking, and * to spread a list into print() or into a new list.

knowledge_points.title: first, *rest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
first, *rest = [5, 8, 2, 9]
print(first, rest)  # 5 [8, 2, 9]
*init, last = [5, 8, 2, 9]
print(init, last)   # [5, 8, 2] 9
The starred name always becomes a list, possibly empty.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values for starred unpacking at the start, middle and end; compare with the equivalent slices.

knowledge_points.title: Star fixes the count mismatch
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name, *others = 'Ada King Lovelace'.split()
print(name, others)  # Ada ['King', 'Lovelace']
head, *_ = (1, 2, 3)
print(head)  # 1
Only one starred name is allowed per assignment.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix unpackings that raise ValueError by adding a star; spot an illegal double star.

knowledge_points.title: Spreading a list with *
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums)    # [1, 2, 3]
print(*nums)   # 1 2 3
print([0, *nums, 4])  # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
*nums passes the items separately, as if you had typed them.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict printed output with and without *; build a combined list with * inside brackets.

topics.title: Using returned tuples: index, ignore and collect results
topics.summary: Work with functions that return several values: index the returned tuple, ignore parts with _, collect results in a list and unpack them in a loop, and keep every return the same shape.

knowledge_points.title: The result is one tuple: keep it or index it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def divide(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b

result = divide(17, 5)
print(result, result[1])  # (3, 2) 2
return a, b builds one tuple; index it when you need only one part.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what printing or indexing a returned tuple shows; choose between unpacking and indexing for a described need.

knowledge_points.title: Ignore values you do not need with _
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def stats(a, b):
    return a + b, a * b, a - b

total, _, diff = stats(6, 2)
print(total, diff)  # 8 4
_ is an ordinary name used by convention for 'not needed'; the number of names must still match.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in unpacking lines that keep only some returned values; fix lines with the wrong number of names.

knowledge_points.title: Collect results in a list, unpack them in a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
results = []
for n in [7, 12]:
    results.append(divide(n, 5))
for q, r in results:
    print(q, r)
# 1 2
# 2 2
Each call adds one tuple; the for loop unpacks them again (divide as in KP1).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that stores several function results and a second loop that unpacks and prints them; predict the output.

knowledge_points.title: Return a flag and a value, with the same shape every time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def find(items, target):
    i = 0
    for item in items:
        if item == target:
            return True, i
        i += 1
    return False, -1

found, pos = find(["a", "b"], "b")
print(found, pos)          # True 1
print(find(["a"], "z"))  # (False, -1)
Every return gives two values, so the caller's unpacking works whatever happens.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a function whose early return gives one value while the other gives two; predict results for found and missing targets.

topics.notes: Reconciliation: replaces unpacking.return_multiple_values, which duplicated return_values.multiple_return_values (B05 owns 'return a, b' and unpacking the result). This topic builds on it.

topics.title: Index and item together with enumerate()
topics.summary: Replace range(len(...)) loops with enumerate to get each position and item, starting the count anywhere.

knowledge_points.title: enumerate gives (index, item) pairs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['Ana', 'Bo']
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(i, name)
# 0 Ana / 1 Bo
Each pass unpacks one (index, item) tuple.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output; rewrite a range(len(...)) loop with enumerate.

knowledge_points.title: Numbering from 1 with start=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for n, task in enumerate(['wash', 'dry'], start=1):
    print(n, task)
# 1 wash / 2 dry
start changes the count only; the items are the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in enumerate so a menu is numbered from 1; predict output for other starts.

knowledge_points.title: Remember where something was
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = [18, 31, 25]
best_i = 0
for i, t in enumerate(temps):
    if t > temps[best_i]:
        best_i = i
print('hottest day', best_i)  # hottest day 1
enumerate keeps the item handy and the index available.
knowledge_points.practice: Write loops that report the position of the max, or of every match.

topics.title: Walking several lists together with zip()
topics.summary: Pair up items from two or more lists with zip, know that it stops at the shortest, and pair each item with the next one.

knowledge_points.title: zip pairs items at the same position
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['Ana', 'Bo']
scores = [91, 78]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)
No index needed: zip hands over matching items together.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a range(len(...)) parallel-list loop with zip; predict output.

knowledge_points.title: zip stops at the shortest list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b'])))  # [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
Extra items are silently dropped; check lengths first if that would be a bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict list(zip(...)) for unequal lengths and for three lists.

knowledge_points.title: Pairing each item with the next
knowledge_points.worked_example:
temps = [18, 21, 19, 25]
for a, b in zip(temps, temps[1:]):
    print(b - a)
# 3 / -2 / 6
temps[1:] is the list shifted by one, so there is no off-by-one to get wrong.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a check that a list is in increasing order with zip; predict pair differences.

topics.title: Two names, one list: aliasing
topics.summary: Predict what happens when two names refer to the same list, and tell mutating a list apart from rebinding a name.

knowledge_points.title: b = a does not copy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
Assignment gives the same list a second name; a change through either name is seen by both.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both lists after changes made through an alias.

knowledge_points.title: Mutating vs rebinding
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b = b + [3]   # + builds a new list; b now names it
print(a, b)    # [1, 2] [1, 2, 3]
append, item assignment and remove change the shared list; = with a new value only moves one name.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify each line as mutating or rebinding; predict both names afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: += on a list mutates the shared list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b += [3]
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3]
For lists, += extends in place, so the alias sees it; b = b + [3] would not.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of += vs + with an alias present.

knowledge_points.title: Immutable values can't surprise you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = 'hi'
t = s
t += '!'
print(s, t)  # hi hi!
n = 1
m = n
m += 1
print(n, m)  # 1 2
Strings, numbers and tuples cannot be changed, so every 'change' makes a new object.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results for the same code with a list, a string and a tuple.

topics.title: Same value or same object: == vs is
topics.summary: Use == to compare contents and is to test whether two names refer to the same object, and know when each is right.

knowledge_points.title: == compares contents, is compares identity
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b)  # True False
print(a == c, a is c)  # True True
b is an equal list, c is the same list.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict == and is for pairs of names created in different ways.

knowledge_points.title: id() shows which object a name refers to
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2]
c = a
print(id(a) == id(c))  # True
print(id(a) == id([1, 2]))  # False
x is y means id(x) == id(y).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether two ids are equal; decide which names would see a mutation.

knowledge_points.title: Use is only for None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
answer = None
if answer is None:
    print('no answer yet')
names = ['Ana']
if names == ['Ana']:  # not: names is ['Ana']
    print('match')
Comparing values with is gives unreliable results; Python even warns (SyntaxWarning) about is with a number or string literal.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix comparisons that wrongly use is; choose the right operator for described checks.

topics.title: Lists passed to functions
topics.summary: Predict when a function changes the caller's list, and choose between mutating it and returning a new list.

knowledge_points.title: The parameter is an alias for the caller's list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_bonus(scores):
    for i in range(len(scores)):
        scores[i] += 5

mine = [70, 80]
add_bonus(mine)
print(mine)  # [75, 85]
No return needed: the function mutated the one shared list.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the caller's list after calling functions that mutate their argument.

knowledge_points.title: Rebinding the parameter does not affect the caller
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def reset(scores):
    scores = []

mine = [70, 80]
reset(mine)
print(mine)  # [70, 80]
scores = [] only moves the local name; scores.clear() would empty the caller's list.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify function bodies as changing or not changing the caller's list; fix a reset function.

knowledge_points.title: Returning a new list keeps the original safe
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def with_bonus(scores):
    result = []
    for s in scores:
        result.append(s + 5)
    return result

mine = [70, 80]
print(with_bonus(mine), mine)  # [75, 85] [70, 80]
Decide per function: mutate in place, or return a new list and leave the input alone.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a mutating function to return a new list; predict both lists afterwards.

topics.title: Making a real copy of a list
topics.summary: Copy a list with [:], list() or .copy() so changes to the copy leave the original alone, and use a copy to loop safely while removing.

knowledge_points.title: Three ways to copy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a[:]
c = list(a)
d = a.copy()
b.append(4)
print(a, b)  # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3, 4]
Each makes a new list with the same items.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both lists after changing a copy vs an alias.

knowledge_points.title: A copy is equal but not identical
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a.copy()
print(a == b, a is b)  # True False
Same contents, separate object.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict == and is for copies and aliases; fix a 'backup' that is really an alias.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over a copy, change the original
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a remove-while-looping bug by adding a copy; choose between this and building a new list.

topics.title: Copies of lists of lists: shallow vs deep
topics.summary: Recognise that copying a list of lists shares the inner lists, and use copy.deepcopy or build fresh rows when that matters.

knowledge_points.title: A list can hold lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(grid[1])     # [3, 4]
print(grid[1][0])  # 3
The first index picks the inner list, the second picks inside it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict single and double indexing into a small grid.

knowledge_points.title: A shallow copy shares the inner lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
copy1 = grid.copy()
copy1[0][0] = 99
print(grid)  # [[99, 2], [3, 4]]
Only the outer list was copied; both outer lists hold the same inner lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the original after changes to a shallow copy (replacing a row vs changing inside a row).

knowledge_points.title: copy.deepcopy copies all the way down
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import copy
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
safe = copy.deepcopy(grid)
safe[0][0] = 99
print(grid)  # [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
Use deepcopy when inner lists will be changed.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose shallow or deep copy for described situations; fix a backup that changes with the original.

knowledge_points.title: The [[0] * 3] * 3 trap
knowledge_points.worked_example:
bad = [[0] * 3] * 3
bad[0][0] = 1
print(bad)  # [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]]
good = []
for _ in range(3):
    good.append([0] * 3)
* repeats references to the same inner list; build each row separately.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the grid after one change; fix grid creation code.

topics.title: Sorting a list: sort() and sorted()
topics.summary: Sort in place with list.sort() or get a new sorted list with sorted(), in either direction, and predict how strings and mixed types sort.

knowledge_points.title: sort() changes the list; sorted() returns a new one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(sorted(nums), nums)  # [1, 2, 3] [3, 1, 2]
nums.sort()
print(nums)                # [1, 2, 3]
Use sorted() to keep the original order; sort() when you no longer need it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list and the result after sort() vs sorted(); choose which one a task needs.

knowledge_points.title: Descending order and reverse()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(sorted(nums, reverse=True))  # [3, 2, 1]
nums.reverse()
print(nums)                       # [2, 1, 3]
reverse=True sorts high to low; reverse() only flips the current order.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of reverse=True vs reverse(); write the call for a high-score table.

knowledge_points.title: x = lst.sort() gives None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
result = nums.sort()
print(result)  # None
sort() is a list method that changes in place and returns None; use sorted() for a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that assigns or prints the result of sort().

knowledge_points.title: How strings and mixed types sort
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(sorted(['bob', 'Amy', 'carl']))  # ['Amy', 'bob', 'carl']
print(sorted(['b', 'B', 'a']))         # ['B', 'a', 'b']
# sorted([3, 'a']) -> TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
Strings sort by character code, so every capital comes before every lower-case letter.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sorted order for mixed-case words and digit strings like '10' vs '9'; spot the TypeError case.

topics.title: Sorting records and sorting by a key
topics.summary: Sort lists of tuples, sort by a different field by reordering tuples, sort by len or case-insensitively with key=, and take the top n.

knowledge_points.title: Tuples sort by the first item, then the next
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pairs = [('Bo', 78), ('Ana', 91), ('Ana', 60)]
print(sorted(pairs))
# [('Ana', 60), ('Ana', 91), ('Bo', 78)]
Sorting uses tuple comparison: ties on the first item are broken by the second.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the sorted order of short lists of tuples.

knowledge_points.title: Sort by another field: put it first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pairs = [('Bo', 78), ('Ana', 91)]
flipped = []
for name, score in pairs:
    flipped.append((score, name))
for score, name in sorted(flipped, reverse=True):
    print(name, score)
Build (score, name) tuples so the field you sort by comes first.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder lines of the flip-sort-print program; write it for a different field.

knowledge_points.title: key= sorts by a computed value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['kiwi', 'Fig', 'banana']
print(sorted(words, key=len))        # ['Fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))  # ['banana', 'Fig', 'kiwi']
key is a function name without (): sorting compares key(item), but returns the original items.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sorts with key=len and key=str.lower; fix key=len() (called by mistake).

knowledge_points.title: Top n: sort, then slice
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [72, 95, 88, 60, 91]
top3 = sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3]
print(top3)  # [95, 91, 88]
Combine a descending sort with a slice for 'best n' and 'worst n' questions.
knowledge_points.practice: Write one-line expressions for the top or bottom n; predict results.
